::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## The end-of-course project goal

Your team answers a predictive question with a public data set, in R and/or Python,
with a focus on reproducible and trustworthy workflows.
**By the end of the course**, your single Quarto document will have become a project with:

-   well-documented, modular scripts in R and/or Python
-   a pipeline automated with GNU Make
-   a reproducible Quarto report
-   a Docker container for the computational environment
-   a GitHub repository for collaboration and sharing
:::

## Milestone 3 summary

This milestone is about moving your analysis code **out of your report and into scripts**,
and checking your data before you use it.

- [ ] Split your analysis into **4 or more scripts** that take [command line arguments]{.term tabindex="0" data-tip="Values you type after the script name when you run it in the terminal, e.g. python scripts/clean.py --input data/raw/data.csv --output data/processed/clean.csv. They let you change inputs and outputs without editing the code."}
- [ ] Add [data validation]{.term tabindex="0" data-tip="Data validation means automatic checks that your data looks the way your analysis expects (the right columns and types, no impossible values, not too many missing values) before you use it. Here the checks run inside your scripts, so a problem stops the analysis early instead of silently giving wrong results."} checks to your scripts
- [ ] Make your report a `.qmd` that **shows** the figures and tables your scripts saved, instead of computing them
- [ ] Add any new packages to your environment and publish a new Docker image
- [ ] Update your `README` so it says how to run each script in the container

::: callout-important
## See what a finished Milestone 3 looks like

Look at its `scripts/` folder and its `README`.
It uses conda for its environment: ignore that part and keep the uv/renv setup from Milestone 2.

## Readings for this milestone

-   [Scripts](https://ubc-dsci.github.io/reproducible-and-trustworthy-workflows-for-data-science/lectures/scripts.html): writing scripts with command line arguments (`click` and `docopt`)
-   [Data validation](https://ubc-dsci.github.io/reproducible-and-trustworthy-workflows-for-data-science/lectures/data-validation.html): what to check, and the checklist you must cover
-   [Data validation with pandera](https://ubc-dsci.github.io/reproducible-and-trustworthy-workflows-for-data-science/lectures/data-validation-python-pandera.html) (Python) or [with pointblank](https://ubc-dsci.github.io/reproducible-and-trustworthy-workflows-for-data-science/lectures/data-validation-r-pointblank.html) (R)
:::

### 1. Move your code into scripts

1.  **Split your analysis into 4 or more scripts** (`.py` or `.R`) in a `scripts/` folder,
    one script per step of the analysis.
    The code doesn't need to be turned into functions yet (that is Milestone 4).
    A common split:
    -   download the data
    -   clean and split the data
    -   exploratory figures and tables
    -   fit the model and evaluate it

2.  **Chain them:** the files one script writes are the files the next script reads.

3.  **Give every script command line arguments** for at least its input path and its output path,
    so nothing is hard-coded.
    Use [`click`](https://click.palletsprojects.com/) in Python, or `docopt` in R.
    Use descriptive file names (`data/processed/cancer_train.csv`, not `data/file.csv`).

4.  **Save every figure and table to a file** (for example in `results/`), so the report can show it.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## What each script could look like

| Script | Reads | Writes |
|---|---|---|
| download | a URL | `data/raw/...` |
| clean and split | the raw data | cleaned train and test files in `data/processed/` |
| EDA | the training data | figures and tables in `results/` |
| model | the training and test data | the fitted model, plus result figures and tables in `results/` |

Running a Python script in the container looks like this (R: `Rscript` instead of `uv run python`):

```bash
docker compose run --rm analysis-env \
  uv run python scripts/download_data.py \
  --url https://example.com/data.csv \
  --write-to data/raw/cancer.csv
```

You can split your code differently, or have more scripts.
What matters is having about 4, so you can practise joining them into a pipeline in Milestone 4.
:::

### 2. Add data validation checks

1.  **Write the checks as code in your scripts**, for example in the script that cleans or splits the data.
2.  **Write at least one check for each item** in the textbook's
    [data validation checklist](https://ubc-dsci.github.io/reproducible-and-trustworthy-workflows-for-data-science/lectures/data-validation.html#data-validation-checklist).
3.  **Decide what happens when a check fails** (stop with an error, or warn and continue), and make the code do that.
4.  **Don't leak test data:** checks that look at relationships between columns (such as correlations)
    run on the training data only.

### 3. Make your report show your scripts' results

1.  If your report is not a `.qmd` yet, convert it:
    `quarto convert report.ipynb` for a Jupyter notebook, or just rename an `.Rmd` file to `.qmd`.
2.  Replace the analysis code in the report with code that **reads and displays** the figures and tables your scripts saved.
3.  Don't polish its formatting yet (cross-references, citations, hidden code): that is Milestone 4.
4.  After you re-render it, copy it to `docs/index.html` again and push,
    so the report on GitHub Pages stays current (see [Milestone 2](milestone2.qmd#publish-your-report-on-github-pages)).

### 4. Update your environment

Your scripts probably use new packages (`click` or `docopt`, a validation package).
Add each one, pinned, the same way you did in Milestone 2:
add it with uv or renv, commit the changed files and push, let GitHub Actions publish a new image
and update the tag in `docker-compose.yml`, then `git pull` and `docker compose pull`.
([uv recap from DSCI 521](https://ubc-mds.github.io/DSCI_521_platforms-dsci_book/lectures/virtual-environments-uv.html))

### 5. Update your `README`

Your `README` must say **how to run each script**, in order, with the exact command and its arguments,
using the container (`docker compose run --rm analysis-env ...`), then how to render the report.

::: callout-important
## 5 all-or-nothing points for your README instructions

If someone can't run each of your scripts and render your report by following your instructions
**exactly as written**, you lose all 5 points.
Test them on **both Windows and Mac**.
If your team doesn't have both, ask another team to test them.
:::

## Submission instructions

1.  Just before you submit, create a GitHub release named exactly `2.0.0`
    ([how to create a release](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/releasing-projects-on-github/managing-releases-in-a-repository#creating-a-release)).
2.  On Gradescope, enter these three URLs (there is no PDF to make):
    -   the GitHub release
    -   your group project's repository (general one without GitHub release)
    -   your report on GitHub Pages
    -   your report on GitHub Pages

You don't need to include Milestone 2 feedback in this submission.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself before submitting

- [ ] At least 4 scripts, each taking its input and output paths as command line arguments
- [ ] Each script reads what the previous one wrote
- [ ] At least one validation check for each item in the data validation checklist, with a planned response when it fails
- [ ] Your report is a `.qmd` that shows saved figures and tables instead of computing them
- [ ] Every new package is pinned, and `docker-compose.yml` uses the new image's `sha-` tag
- [ ] Someone on Windows and someone on Mac followed your `README` steps exactly
- [ ] Your report on GitHub Pages matches your release
- [ ] No generated files committed by mistake (except `docs/`, which GitHub Pages needs)
- [ ] You created the `2.0.0` release
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Teamwork expectations (these are marked)

-   **Everyone contributes equally** to code, writing and project management,
    shown by a roughly equal number of commits, pull request reviews and GitHub issue comments.
-   Use the [GitHub flow](https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/using-github/github-flow):
    a branch for each feature or fix, reviewed by at least one teammate before the pull request is merged.
-   Commit and push every time you work on the project, with meaningful commit messages
    (one or two less meaningful ones are OK).
-   Talk to your teammates in GitHub issues, not email or Slack:
    at least 3 issues per person on average in this milestone.
-   Your question, analysis and visualization should make sense. They don't have to be complicated.
-   Your analysis should be correct and run reproducibly from your `README` instructions.
-   Follow the [black style guide](https://black.readthedocs.io/en/stable/the_black_code_style/index.html) (Python)
    or the [tidyverse style guide](https://style.tidyverse.org/) (R).
-   Write your `README` in full sentences with proper grammar. Keep point form under 10% of it.
:::
